blocks.text: And Pantaleon the deacon, in his sermon On the Holy Lights: Ὁ τοῖς τῶν μελισσῶν κατὰ τὴν ἔρημον πόνοις, καὶ τοῖς τῶν βοτανῶν συντρεφόμενος ἐκ βρέφους ἀκρίσμασι· [Ho tois tōn melissōn kata tēn erēmon ponois, kai tois tōn botanōn syntrephomenos ek brephous akrismasi] [III, 327] He who from infancy was nourished on the labours of the bees in the desert and on the tips of herbs. And Theophylact: Τινὲς δὲ (λέγουσι) τὰ ἀκρόδρυα, ἤτοι ὀπώρας ἀγρίας (εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας·) [Tines de (legousi) ta akrodrya, ētoi opōras agrias (einai tas akridas)] Some say that the acridas are the tips of trees, or wild fruits. And Euthymius: But some have said that the locusts were shoots of herbs. And Nicephorus Callistus, History book 1, chapter 14: There he used for food the tenderer tops of trees, ἄκροις δρυῶν [akrois dryōn]. And in the last century Cajetan: I suspect that the name is equivocal, applying both to those animals, locusts, and to roots, or the tender tops of shrubs or twigs, or something of this kind that we eat raw. Swept away by this torrent, Baronius, under the year 31, says: What we should think of these things is not for us to decide; we leave the whole matter to the reader's judgement. For it is agreed that the Greek word ἀκρίδας [akridas] signifies both the locust, a kind of insect [col. 489] having weak wings for flying, and the tops of trees. On the contrary, it is agreed that ἀκρίδας [akridas] and ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya] differ greatly, and that these two words are nowhere confused by truly Greek writers. Yet those of the ancients who shrank from eating locusts did this all the more readily because they knew that ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya] had served some people as food. Thus in the Paedagogus of Clement, book 2, ch. 1, the apostle Matthew σπερμάτων, καὶ ἀκροδρύων, καὶ λαχάνων, ἄνευ κρέων, μετελάμβανεν [spermatōn, kai akrodryōn, kai lachanōn, aneu kreōn, metelambanen], ate seeds, and tops of trees, and vegetables, without meat. But in the same place John is distinguished from Matthew precisely by the fact that ὑπερτείνας τὴν ἐγκράτειαν, ἀκρίδας, καὶ μέλι ἤσθιεν ἄγριον [hyperteinas tēn enkrateian, akridas, kai meli ēsthien agrion], carrying abstinence further, he ate locusts and wild honey. So you may know that for him ἀκρίδας [akridas] were one thing and ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya] another. Thus in the age of Epiphanius some were so rigid in their fasts that they abstained even from ἀκροδρύων, καὶ ἑψημάτων [akrodryōn, kai hepsēmatōn], from the tops of trees and from vegetable broths, as though this were too much. So he says in the Exposition of the Faith, ch. 23. The third opinion is that of those for whom αἱ ἀκρίδες [hai akrides] are a kind of herb. Euthymius: But some have said that the locusts were shoots of herbs, and others a herb called locust. Theophylact: Τινὲς λέγουσι βοτάνας εἶναι τὰς ἀκρίδας, ἃς καὶ μέλαγρα καλοῦσι· [Tines legousi botanas einai tas akridas, has kai melagra kalousi] Some say that the acridas are herbs, which they also call melagra, as an allusion to μέλι ἄγριον [meli agrion]. So, on this opinion, the honey and the locusts will be the same thing: namely a kind of herb otherwise entirely unknown, which nevertheless alone sufficed John for food. Nothing more absurd could be imagined. Yet even this opinion had its followers, among them Surianus, a monk, from whom Jacques de Vitry, ch. 53 of the History of Jerusalem, professes to have learned that the ἀκρίδας [akridas] of John were not locusts but a certain herb that used to be served to monks in Syria. Perhaps also Dionysius the Carthusian, who writes that some understand by locusts herbs of the desert, since it does not seem probable that John, who did not even eat bread, ate the flesh of animals or anything cooked. And Hermolaus, on Dioscorides, Corollary 256, says that the herb meant is the one called in Arabic رجل الجراد [rijl al-jarād] locust's foot; that is, blitum [blite], as some hold, or, as [III, 328] others, rapunculum [rampion]. Let the fourth opinion be the one that holds the ἀκρίδας [akridas] of John to be little birds. Christian Druthmar, who wrote on Matthew in the ninth century after Christ: About the locusts I have heard someone say that these locusts were small birds with red legs. This would be tolerable if he had said only winged creatures, for among flying locusts some have red feet. But since he said a little bird with red feet, what else are we to understand than the ἐρυθρόποδα [erythropoda] of the Greeks? They take it to be a species of finch. That Druthmar understood a real bird is certainly clear, since he refutes the author of this opinion thus: Why would (John) be praised for the rigour of his abstinence, if he ate the flying creatures that the Jews longed for? The fifth: that the locusts were sea fish, which John obtained from the Jordan, as the same Druthmar reports, which is quite ridiculous. For these locusts are found not in rivers but in the sea itself. Not to mention that sea locusts [lobsters] are called by the Greeks not ἀκρίδας [akridas] but καράβους [karabous]. Finally, since sea locusts are counted a delicacy, here too Druthmar rightly objects that there would be no reason to praise John for abstinence if he ate marine delicacies. The same objection can be raised against those who change ἀκρίδας [akridas] into καρίδας [karidas], that is, squillas [shrimps], than which nothing in the whole crab family is more excellent. To this opinion, which is the sixth, I add a seventh, that of a very great and most pious man, who conjectures that the Evangelists here wrote ἀχράδες [achrades], that is, wild pears, and that by a slight change this word was turned into ἀκρίδες [akrides] ^{(1)}.
